new_statements.translation: Franke: 'In all Germanic languages the stem syllable carries the word accent. As a result, at the end of the OHG period the vowels of the formative syllables were reduced to e or æ.' Goepfert: 'As regards the accentuation of compounds, as in NHG the main stress always lies on the first part, the secondary stress on the second; here too words compounded with an inseparable particle are an exception.'

Because of this potential for ambiguity, stress is transcribed in all polysyllabic examples in this entry.' followed by the Kuegler/Selting/Peters/Gilles p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress works as in Standard German: native words stress the root/stem syllable, which in mono- and disyllabic native roots surfaces as initial (or penultimate) stress; unstressed prefixes (be-, ge-, ver- etc.) and inflectional/derivational endings are unstressed and heavily reduced; loanwords and polymorphemic words may carry stress elsewhere (Leipzig speech even retracts stress to the first syllable in some loans, Albrecht 1881 §149); compounds take main stress on the first member, secondary on the second, inseparable-prefix formations excepted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Goepfert 1878: 63 — in compounds the Nebenton falls on the second member. Khan & Weise say nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Borrowed and polymorphemic words can have other patterns (Khan & Weise); inseparable-prefix words do not take initial main stress (Goepfert); Leipzig dialect shifts stress to the first syllable in loans like Bureau, Bazar, Cacao, Papa and to the ending in -ik/-iker words (Albrecht 1881 §149).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress; Khan & Weise mark stress on every polysyllabic word in citation forms and in the connected North Wind passage. Franke §7 separately describes the characteristic two-peaked rising-falling syllable/word pitch contour of Meissnisch ('singing' accent), which concerns tonal realisation, not stress position.
new_statements.identity_note: Khan & Weise 2013 describe the urban Chemnitz variety (Vorerzgebirgisch), which they and Bergmann 1990 place as transitional between Meissnisch, Vogtländisch and Erzgebirgisch but treat as Upper Saxon; it falls under uppe1400. Franke 1884 covers Meissnisch/Osterländisch/Dessau-Herzberg Upper Saxon proper (core uppe1400). Goepfert 1878 is West Erzgebirgisch (Annaberg/Marienberg), an Upper Saxon–East Franconian transition zone, so it is supporting evidence only. Glottolog's uppe1400 'Central East Middle German' also subsumes Thuringian and some Silesian/Transylvanian refs; the statement quoted is for Upper Saxon.

tone_statements.citation: Siebenhaar, Beat. 2012. Warum glauben wir, dass Dialektsprecher 'singen'? Zur Erforschung der Sprechmelodien in den Dialekten [preprint title: Wie 'singen' Dialektsprecher? – Zur Erforschung der Sprechmelodien in den Dialekten]. In Rainer Hünecke & Karlheinz Jakob (eds.), Die obersächsische Sprachlandschaft in Geschichte und Gegenwart (Sprache – Literatur und Geschichte 42), 265-288. Heidelberg: Universitätsverlag Winter.
tone_statements.quote: Gericke hat in einer frühen instrumentalphonetischen Arbeit zur Intonation der Leipziger Umgangssprache spezifische Intonationsverläufe herausgearbeitet, die sie als nach oben gerichtete Bogenform oder Fallbogen beschreibt. Diese Besonderheit wird in neueren Untersuchungen für Dresden bestätigt. [...] In Dresden und Mannheim findet sich je eine zusätzliche Kontur. In Dresden ist dies der schon von Gericke beschriebene Fallbogen, wo der hohe Ton gehalten wird und der Fall erst verzögert am Schluss der Äußerung stattfindet (sound10).
tone_statements.translation: In an early instrumental-phonetic study of the intonation of Leipzig colloquial speech, Gericke worked out specific intonation contours, which she describes as an upward-directed arch or 'Fallbogen' (falling arch). This peculiarity is confirmed for Dresden in more recent studies. [...] In Dresden and Mannheim one additional contour each is found. In Dresden this is the Fallbogen already described by Gericke, in which the high tone is held and the fall takes place only late, at the end of the utterance (sound10).
tone_statements.locator: preprint section 2 'Historische Belege' (p.4) and section 3.1 on intonation contours (p.10); see also p.7 (Becker/Bergmann pitch-height claim rejected) and p.18 (timing)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; regional specificity lies in post-lexical intonation contours (Leipzig/Dresden Fallbogen: held high pitch with late final fall) and in accent-peak alignment, not in any word-level pitch contrast.

tone_statements.citation: Kleber, Felicitas & Tamara Rathcke. 2008. More on the "segmental anchoring" of prenuclear rises: Evidence from East Middle German. In Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2008, Campinas, Brazil, 583-586. ISCA. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2008-132
tone_statements.quote: The regional variety chosen for the present investigation is Upper Saxon spoken in East Middle German. Henceforth, we only use the term East Middle German (EG) which is the hypernym for Upper Saxon [...]. Informal auditory observations of EG intonation suggested that prenuclear, but also nuclear accents are always aligned late in the accented syllable. The prenuclear rise sounds like both being very long and reaching the target position quite late (for a detailed description of Saxon intonation see [11]). [...] Our results show that L is aligned earlier in East Middle German than in Northern and Southern German and that left-sided time pressure effects the alignment of L, but not of H.
tone_statements.locator: section 1 Introduction, p.583; abstract p.583; speakers section 2.3 p.584
tone_statements.summary: Intonation language like Standard German: pitch accents (L*+H prenuclear rises) associate with stressed syllables; the regional property is phonetic alignment of tonal targets, not a lexical pitch contrast.

tone.quote: Biester hob hervor, dass sogar bei Oberschichtsprechern das unangenehme Singen, das mir statt wir auffalle, und „die höchstseltsame Verwechslung des b und p, des d und t sehr gewöhnlich“ seien.

tone.translation: Biester stressed that even among upper-class speakers the unpleasant sing-song, 'mir' for 'wir', and 'the most peculiar confusion of b and p, of d and t' were quite usual.

tone.quote: Der Dresdener Fallbogen beginnt typischerweise mit einem H*- oder L*+>H-Nukleusakzent, der Fall selbst und ein späterer H-Ton wird auf unakzentuierten postnuklearen Silben realisiert. ... Überblick über die Dresdener Intonation: Im Dresdenerischen werden in vielen Kontexten und Aktivitätstypen oftmals die gleichen Konturen verwendet wie im Standarddeutschen. Daneben fallen aber in den Daten einige saliente Konturen auf, die für diese Stadtsprache typisch zu sein scheinen.
tone.locator: p. 8, end of section 2 'Forschungsstand' and section 3 'Überblick über die Dresdener Intonation'
tone.translation: The Dresden 'Fallbogen' typically begins with an H* or L*+>H nuclear accent; the fall itself and a later H tone are realised on unaccented postnuclear syllables. ... Overview of Dresden intonation: In Dresden speech, in many contexts and activity types the same contours are often used as in Standard German. In addition, however, some salient contours stand out in the data that seem to be typical of this urban variety.
tone.summary: No lexical tone: intonation language like Standard German; post-lexical pitch accents (H*, L*+>H) dock on word-stress syllables; regionally salient Dresden 'Fallbogen' contour H* H ^L% (emphasis); 'flat' overall melody.

sources.note: Secondhand via Selting 2002b: 6: collects linguists' statements on the typical Saxon intonation — rather tensionless, flat base melody with soft contours, average declarative interval a third; the 'singing' attributed to stressed syllables being spoken higher; further a 'zweigipfliger Silbentonwechsel' (two-peaked syllable pitch movement), vowel overlength and Gericke's Fallbogen named as characteristic of Saxon (Zimmermann 1998: 8). A literature digest, not an analysis; no lexical tone claim.
